summary: Specifies how to use IKE to set up IPsec security associations without authenticating the peer, an approach called Better-Than-Nothing Security. No wire format changes to IKEv2 are needed, though some database extensions are defined. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Sometimes you can lock the door without checking who is on the other side. It does not tell you who it is, but it still stops eavesdroppers from reading along.

subtitle: How to set up IPsec without checking who the other side is, so traffic is at least protected from eavesdroppers.

tldr.problem: IPsec normally needs the peers to be configured with each other's identities or certificates, which is often not practical, so many connections stay completely unprotected.
tldr.mechanism: BTNS adds a PUBLICKEY identity type, a catch-all last entry in the Peer Authorization Database, and a BTNS_OK flag on Security Policy Database entries, so IKEv2 can set up SAs with any peer that proves it holds a private key.
tldr.outcome: Traffic gets IPsec protection without knowing who the peer is. It remains open to man-in-the-middle attacks unless higher layers add authentication.

facts.label: Key type with a CERT payload

today: RFC 5386 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its companion applicability statement is RFC 5387.

sections.title: What BTNS Is
sections.content:
RFC 5386 describes how to establish unauthenticated IPsec security associations (SAs) using IKEv2 and unauthenticated public keys. The popular name for this is BTNS, short for Better-Than-Nothing Security. The SAs can be used with both the ESP and AH parts of IPsec.

No new on-the-wire protocol elements are added to IKEv2. The change is in how a node decides whether to accept a peer: the Peer Authorization Database (PAD) and the Security Policy Database (SPD) of the RFC 4301 processing model are extended.

The document does not define an opportunistic mode that falls back to unprotected IP, and it does not describe leap-of-faith modes or connection latching. Those are left to RFC 5387 and other work.
sections.eli5: Normally a guard checks your name badge before letting you in. BTNS says: if nobody can check badges, still use a private tunnel so outsiders cannot listen in.

sections.title: The PUBLICKEY ID and BTNS PAD Entries
sections.content:
The RFC adds a new ID type, PUBLICKEY, whose value is a public key. It is never sent on the wire. PAD entries that match on PUBLICKEY IDs are called BTNS PAD entries; all others are non-BTNS PAD entries.

A BTNS PAD entry may match specific peer public keys (or their fingerprints) or all peer public keys. The latter is the wildcard BTNS PAD entry. At most one wildcard entry may appear, and it MUST be the last entry in the PAD.

Any peer that uses an IKEv2 AUTH method based on a digital signature may match a BTNS entry, as long as it matches no non-BTNS entry. The RFC names RSA Digital Signature (method #1) and DSS Digital Signature (method #3) as suitable methods as of August 2007. A node that wants to be treated as a BTNS node MUST include bare public key CERT payloads, and only bare RSA keys are defined, so BTNS works only with RSA public keys.
sections.eli5: The guest list has named guests first and, at the very bottom, a line that says anyone with a key that fits the lock may come in. The key proves you can open it, not who you are.

sections.title: How Peers Are Matched
sections.content:
A BTNS-capable implementation first searches the PAD for non-BTNS entries matching the peer's asserted ID. If none match, the peer's ID MUST be coerced to type PUBLICKEY with the peer's public key as its value, and the PAD is searched again for BTNS entries. A single search that gives the same result is allowed. If nothing matches at all, the IKE SA is rejected as usual.

A peer that matches a BTNS entry is a BTNS peer. It is still checked, in a narrow sense: its signature in the IKEv2 AUTH payload is verified with the public key from its CERT payload. That proves possession of the private key, not a real-world identity.

Nodes MUST reject IKE_SA proposals from peers that match non-BTNS PAD entries but fail to authenticate properly. So a rogue node cannot fall through to the BTNS entry by claiming a known peer's identity and failing.
sections.eli5: First the guard looks for your name on the list. Only if you are not on it does he check whether your key fits the lock. If you claim to be a named guest and fail, you are thrown out, not let in as a stranger.

sections.title: The BTNS_OK Flag and Access Control Rules
sections.content:
SPD entries get a new flag, BTNS_OK. Traffic to or from peers that match a BTNS PAD entry can match only SPD entries that have this flag set. The SPD may be searched by address or by ID; searching by ID for a BTNS peer needs SPD entries bound to public key values, which could be used to build leap-of-faith behaviour.

To keep normal IPsec access control meaning, three rules apply: BTNS entries MUST logically follow all non-BTNS entries, the wildcard BTNS entry MUST be last, and the wildcard entry MUST have ID constraints that do not logically overlap those of other PAD entries.

The non-overlap rule can be implemented with a second PAD search when BTNS peers negotiate child SAs, to make sure their asserted traffic selectors do not conflict with non-BTNS entries. This stops a BTNS peer from impersonating a non-BTNS peer's addresses.
sections.eli5: Strangers are only allowed into rooms marked "strangers welcome", and never into the rooms reserved for named guests.

sections.title: Worked Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC (informatively) walks through three configurations on a reference network. In the first, a security gateway SG-A has PAD rules for peer B's network and for host Q, followed by PUBLICKEY:any as the BTNS catch-all. A BTNS host C matches only the catch-all and is then matched against an SPD entry flagged BTNS_OK, so it gets transport-mode ESP protection.

A rogue BTNS node asserting Q's or B's addresses either matches their PAD entries and fails to authenticate, or matches the catch-all but is not allowed to create child SAs with those addresses. A rogue node asserting C's own address can succeed, because protecting C needs further binding of its public key to its traffic through connection latching and channel binding or leap-of-faith.

In the second example, Q is an NFSv4 server that protects all traffic with A and also lets any BTNS-capable node negotiate an SA to port 2049. In the third, a BTNS-only node C protects NFSv4 traffic on port 2049 and sends everything else in the clear.
sections.eli5: A building has a list of named visitors with their own rooms, and a lobby open to any stranger who carries a key. Strangers can use the lobby but cannot pretend to be a named visitor.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Unauthenticated security association negotiation is subject to man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks and should be used with care. Where security infrastructure is lacking, the RFC says this may indeed be better than nothing.

One defence is connection latching, where upper-layer protocols cooperate with IPsec to bind packet flows to sequences of similar SAs; it requires native IPsec implementations. MITMs can also be detected with application-layer authentication such as GSS-API with channel binding. How these work is not specified in this document.

Leap of faith means accepting a key on first contact and remembering it, as Secure Shell clients do. For BTNS, the RFC says it was still being designed by the IETF BTNS working group.
sections.eli5: A locked door with no ID check keeps out people walking by, but a clever trickster could still stand between you and your friend. Extra checks later can catch that.
